title: The average is not your outcome
lede: A coin flip that adds 50 % or takes 40 % has a positive expected value. Played over and over with everything reinvested, the typical player is all but wiped out. One hundred players, one hundred rounds, counted.

commit.title: YOUR £
commit.prompt: What is left of £100 for the typical player after 100 rounds, everything reinvested?

captions: The bet: heads turns £100 into £150; tails, into £60.
“It averages £105. Positive expected value: keep going.”
Play it 100 times. Everything stays in the pot.
What is left of £100 for the typical player?
Every win-loss pair multiplies by 0.9, in either order.
The typical run: 50 heads, 50 tails. × 0.9, fifty times.
£100 becomes 52p. At true scale, a hairline.
Now 100 players, £100 each, the same coin.
The line is the expected value. The bars are the players.
87 of 100 lost money. 55 have less than £1 left.
The middle player has 52p. The line says £13,150.
Monday: what does one of us end with if we repeat it?
Limit: a coin game. Bet a fixed sum and the average holds.

brand.takeaway: The average is not your outcome.

monday.q: IF WE REPEAT THIS AND REINVEST EVERYTHING, WHAT DOES ONE OF US END WITH?
monday.limit: A coin game, not a market. Bet a fixed sum, or a fraction, and the result changes.

sources: Peters, O. (2019). The ergodicity problem in economics. Nature Physics 15, 1216–1221. doi:10.1038/s41567-019-0732-0
Peters, O. & Gell-Mann, M. (2016). Evaluating gambles using dynamics. Chaos 26, 023103. doi:10.1063/1.4940236 (arXiv:1405.0585)

Peters, O. (2023). Insurance as an ergodicity problem. Annals of Actuarial Science 17, 215–218. doi:10.1017/S1748499523000131 (Fig. 2: 100 realisations of the same coin toss under the expected-wealth curve)
Kelly, J. L. Jr. (1956). A new interpretation of information rate. Bell System Technical Journal 35(4), 917–926. doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x
Doctor, J. N., Wakker, P. P. & Wang, T. V. (2020). Economists' views on the ergodicity problem. Nature Physics 16, 1168. doi:10.1038/s41567-020-01106-x

This film's seeded simulation: 100 players × 100 rounds, mulberry32(seed 1), draws round by round (for each round, for each player), heads iff the draw < 0.5. Seed 1 is the first seed; its counts sit near the exact binomial expectations (87 vs 86.4 lost money; 55 vs 54.0 under £1).
honest: The coin game is a thought experiment: independent fair flips with fixed payoffs. Real returns are not coin flips, and this is not investment advice.

The drag needs compounding: everything reinvested every round. Bet a fixed sum each round and the average is a fair guide; bet a fraction of the pot and the typical outcome changes (here a quarter of the pot each round makes the typical player grow about 0.6 % a round, Kelly 1956).

The rising line is the expected value, an infinitely large crowd. A real group of 1,000 players does not reach it: across 2,000 seeds the realised average of 1,000 players after 100 rounds had a median of 24×, not 131.5×.
Whether this overturns expected-utility economics is disputed (Doctor, Wakker & Wang 2020). The film claims only the arithmetic of the coin game.

tryit.title: Try it
